title: The Morning Brief: Trade war opens, Syria sanctioned, visa revocations loom
dek: The U.S. and Canada entered open tariff conflict over the weekend, with 50% duties on $20 billion in Canadian goods now in effect and matching retaliation set for early September. Meanwhile, the administration moved on multiple immigration and foreign policy fronts: removing Syria from terrorism lists, preparing mass visa revocations, and deepening sanctions on Iran.
author: GoCheckMyNews
key_fact: A trade dispute with America's second-largest trading partner is now live, with both sides committed to retaliatory measures in September. Federal Reserve officials are already warning the tariffs could extend U.S. inflation, even as the administration pursues broader shifts in immigration enforcement and Middle East policy.
bottom_line: Trade war with Canada is now open, with retaliatory measures scheduled for early September and auto tariffs threatened for January. The Trump administration is simultaneously pursuing the largest mass visa revocation in U.S. history, removing Syria from terrorism sanctions after 47 years, and deepening economic pressure on Iran with new sanctions. Federal Reserve officials are already flagging inflation risks from the tariff conflict. Watch for the formal visa revocation announcement in coming weeks, any resumption of U.S.-Canada trade talks before September 8, and whether Iran follows through on threats to block Persian Gulf oil shipments.
body: The defining story of the weekend is the collapse of U.S.-Canada trade negotiations and the immediate enforcement of tariffs. Late Friday, negotiations failed before a midnight deadline, triggering 50% tariffs on $20 billion in Canadian products, dairy, beverages, cement, and hockey equipment, effective immediately. Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney announced matching retaliatory tariffs on American steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp, paper, and electronics, set to take effect the Tuesday after Labour Day, which falls on September 8. The administration also threatened an additional 50% tariff on Canadian automobiles and parts, effective in January, contingent on no negotiated resolution by then.

Minneapolis Federal Reserve President Neel Kashkari warned Sunday that prolonged tariff disputes extend U.S. inflation pressures. Speaking on Face the Nation, Kashkari said the longer trade conflicts persist, "the imprint and inflation end up being extended and delayed." He cited both the Canada standoff and the Iran conflict as examples of supply shocks that keep inflation elevated. The two countries exchanged $880 billion in goods and services in 2025, per the reporting, making the disruption material to both economies.

The tariff escalation sits alongside a series of administration moves on immigration and foreign policy. The State Department is preparing to revoke B1 and B2 visitor visas for up to 200,000 foreigners who have applied for or are seeking asylum, according to State Department officials. The visas targeted were issued between 2016 and 2026, and the revocation would mark the largest mass visa cancellation in U.S. history, expected to be announced in coming weeks. Deputy Secretary Christopher Landau characterized asylum claims filed after entry on tourist visas as "bogus," saying "asylum isn't supposed to be a loophole to circumvent immigration law." The visa revocation is part of a broader 18-month enforcement push in which the State Department has already revoked about 175,000 visas for people convicted or accused of crimes or who have spoken publicly against U.S. policies.

On Syria, the Trump administration removed the country from its state sponsors of terrorism designation Monday, ending a 47-year designation imposed in 1979. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the move recognizes Syria's government distancing itself from international terrorism. The removal lifts financial sanctions and restrictions on U.S. foreign aid and defense exports, opening the door to private sector investment. Syria's transitional government, led by Ahmad al-Sharaa's Hayat Tahrir al-Sham, now dominates the administration following the late-2024 overthrow of Bashar al-Assad. With Syria's removal, only Cuba, North Korea, and Iran remain on the state sponsors list.

On Iran, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced sweeping new sanctions Monday, calling the measures "Operation Economic Outcast." Bessent said the objective is to "sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone." The sanctions target brokers, companies, and shadow fleet vessels across the UAE, Hong Kong, China, Singapore, Switzerland, and Europe. Iran's security chief vowed "seismic" retaliation and threatened to block oil tanker transit through the Persian Gulf. Iran's currency hit a record low Monday as traders anticipated the sanctions: the rial dropped to 2.02 million to the dollar on informal currency markets where most Iranians conduct business, compared to the official Central Bank rate of around 1.5 million rials to the dollar.

Domestically, the weekend also saw the conviction record in the Sonya Massey case close. Sean Grayson, the former Sangamon County Sheriff's deputy convicted of second-degree murder for her July 2024 shooting death, died in Illinois prison on August 23 while six months into his 20-year sentence. Grayson had been battling colon cancer and the Illinois Prisoner Review Board rejected his medical release request in July 2026. Grayson shot Massey during a welfare call after she made a religious comment he perceived as threatening; his partner at the scene later testified he was not afraid of Massey but feared Grayson's response.
